## Chapter 1

Minister Adams troubled himself little about what he did not see of an enemy; his son, a nervous animal, made life a terror by seeing too much. The father played his hand as it came, and had nothing to lose by making a friend of Russell, while acting always as though Russell were false. Whether Russell were true or false mattered less than the necessity of treating him as if he were false—above all when ironclad rams were rising, under the Lairds’ sheds, before the Government’s eyes. No one could be so simple as to believe that two armored ships-of-war could be built publicly and go to sea like the Alabama without active and incessant collusion. The longer Russell wore the mask of ignorance, the more violently in the end the Minister must tear it off.

As the spring of 1863 drew on, the vast field cleared itself. A campaign better suited to train the mind of a youth eager for training seldom unrolled itself before a young man perched in so commanding a position. After two years of solitude one felt the first faint flush of new and imperial life. At moments one’s breath came quick; one dreamed the sensation of wielding power; then vertigo passed, leaving the brain a little dazed. With an intensity more painful than any Shakespearean drama, men’s eyes were fastened on the armies. Somewhere behind the chaos in Washington, power was taking shape, massed and guided as it had not been before. Yet the diplomatic campaign had to wait for the military to lead. The student could only study.

When the huge blows began to fall with the precision of machinery—Vicksburg and Gettysburg—Londoners were stupid with unbelief. They were learning from the Yankees how to fight. That Sunday the news reached town, and Henry Adams, going early to a small evening reception to exchange a word of congratulation, found the men still over their wine. Presently they came in; Delane of the Times first. One host, with a whoop, threw both arms round the young American’s neck and kissed him on both cheeks. Adams, for once, was not thinking of himself but of Delane, whose eye caught his at the moment of embrace. The British mind is the slowest of all minds; the capture of Vicksburg had not yet penetrated Delane’s thick cortex of fixed ideas. Adams would have liked to warn him: “You come next!”

For nearly a year the private secretary had watched the board arranging itself for collision between the Legation and Delane, who stood behind the Palmerston Ministry. Mr. Adams was steadily strengthened from Washington; the work was well done; the press well organized; the consular staff active; the legal support efficient; social allies swarmed; all that was needed was victory in the field, which Stanton undertook. At the end of July, 1863, the Minister was ready to deal with Russell or Palmerston or Gladstone or Delane, or any one else who stood in his way.

No more volunteer skirmishing was needed. All a secretary could gain now was experience—the measure of men, their motives, foresight, and tenacity. In the Legation no great confidence was felt in stopping the rams. Russell seemed immovable. Little by little the Minister raised his tone, until at last, after stripping Russell of every rag of defence and excuse, he closed by leaving him loaded with connivance in the rebel armaments, and ended with the famous sentence: “It would be superfluous in me to point out to your lordship that this is war!”

What the Minister meant by it was his affair; what the private secretary understood was matter of education. To his copying eye, though on the extreme verge of diplomatic propriety, the words merely stated a fact. The war was Russell’s war—Adams only accepted it.

On September 8, Russell’s reply reached Portland Place: “instructions have been issued which will prevent the departure of the two ironclad vessels from Liverpool.” The modest Legation accepted it as Grant accepted Vicksburg. As Stanton had crushed the rebel left on the Mississippi, so Seward crushed the rebel right in England. Adams never doubted the nature of the battle. The English campaign seemed as creditable to the State Department as Vicksburg to the War Department—well planned, prepared, executed. After a long and desperate struggle, the American Minister had trumped the best card and won the game.

Again and again, in after life, he went back to detect error. He found none. All the more was he disconcerted that Russell, with growing energy to his dying day, denied the axiom of Adams’s whole contention, that from the first he meant to break up the Union. Russell affirmed that he meant nothing of the sort; that he had meant to do right; that he did not know what he meant; and—worse for the student of education—he proved it.

Not till long after Russell’s death did the question reopen. During the Alabama controversy and Geneva in 1872, Russell had been sharply criticised; England paid more than £3,000,000 for his errors. Yet when his biography appeared in 1889, it brought evidence tending to prove that he had been feeble, timid, mistaken, senile—but not dishonest. The Lairds had built in reliance on the known opinion of the law-officers that the statute did not apply and a jury would not convict. Minister Adams rejoined that in that case the statute should be amended, or the ships stopped by political power. Bethell replied that this would be a violation of neutrality; one must preserve the status quo. Tacitly Russell connived, and allowed the builders to go on till the ships were ready for sea. Then, on September 3—two days before the “superfluous” letter—he wrote to Palmerston begging help: “The conduct of the gentlemen who have contracted for the two ironclads at Birkenhead is so very suspicious, that I have thought it necessary to direct that they should be detained,” not under the statute, but on the American ground of international obligation above the statute. “The Solicitor General has been consulted and concurs in the measure as one of policy though not of strict law. We shall thus test the law, and, if we have to pay damages, we have satisfied the opinion which prevails here as well as in America that that kind of neutral hostility should not be allowed to go on without some attempt to stop it.”

For naïveté unusual even in an unpaid attaché, this sudden leap to his opponent’s ground might have roused Palmerston’s scorn; instead he showed loyalty, found “no lawful ground for meddling,” and suggested buying the ships for the Navy. Russell then neglected to notify the American Minister. He should have done so at once on September 3. Instead he waited till the 4th and merely said the matter was under “serious and anxious consideration.” The note did not reach Portland Place till three o’clock on the afternoon of September 5—after the “superfluous” declaration had gone. Thus Russell sacrificed the Lairds; cost his Ministry the price of two ironclads, besides the Alabama Claims; and put himself in the position of appearing to yield only to a threat of war. Finally he wrote to the Admiralty a letter that, from the American point of view, would have sounded youthful from an Eton schoolboy:—

September 14, 1863. MY DEAR DUKE:—

It is of the utmost importance and urgency that the ironclads building at Birkenhead should not go to America to break the blockade. They belong to Monsieur Bravay of Paris. If you will offer to buy them on the part of the Admiralty you will get money’s worth if he accepts your offer; and if he does not, it will be presumptive proof that they are already bought by the Confederates. I should state that we have suggested to the Turkish Government to buy them; but you can easily settle that matter with the Turks....

Had the secretaries seen this letter then, their hilarity would have been loud. Yet these papers upset, from top to bottom, the results of the private secretary’s diplomatic education forty years after he supposed it complete. They made a picture he had not conceived, and rendered worthless his painful experience.

One remark of Gladstone’s, several times repeated, gave him matter for thought: “I always hold that politicians are the men whom, as a rule, it is most difficult to comprehend.... For my own part, I never have thus understood, or thought I understood, above one or two.” Earl Russell was certainly not one of the two. Henry Adams thought he also had understood one or two; but the American type was more familiar. Perhaps this was the sufficient result of his diplomatic education; it seemed to be the whole.

## Chapter 2

Knowledge of human nature is the beginning and end of political education; but several years of arduous study in the neighborhood of Westminster led Henry Adams to think that knowledge of English human nature had little or no value outside of England. The English mind was one-sided, eccentric, systematically unsystematic, logically illogical. For him—the less English education he got, the better.

From the old-world point of view, the American had no mind; he had an economic thinking-machine that could work only on a fixed line. The American mind exasperated the European as a buzz-saw might exasperate a pine forest. The English disliked the French mind because it was antagonistic, but recognized it as a thought; the American mind, to them, was a convention, superficial, narrow, ignorant; a mere cutting instrument, practical, economical, sharp, direct.

The defect that most struck an American was England’s enormous waste in eccentricity. The commonest phrase at club or dinner-table was that So-and-So “is quite mad.” It hardly distinguished him. Thackeray maintained he was no satirist; his pictures were exact and good-natured. Dickens’s extravagance, his audience thought, lay in manner, not type. Mr. Gladstone went to see Sothern act Dundreary and laughed till his face was distorted—not because Dundreary was exaggerated, but because he was ridiculously like figures that might be seen in any club in Pall Mall. Society swarmed with exaggerated characters; it contained little else.

Often this eccentricity bore marks of strength; Boston called it national character—vigor—honesty—courage—and respected it. Yet contact with it in the shape of Palmerston, Russell, and Gladstone made a secretary hesitate. His own type—his father, Weed, Evarts—showed itself not the weaker. Russell might be dishonest or obtuse; the English type brutal or only stupid; but strong, in either case, it was not, nor did it seem strong to Englishmen.

In private society, eccentricity made the chief charm and the chief terror. Barring atrocious insolence which Englishmen and especially Englishwomen showed to each other—rarely to foreigners—society was more easy and tolerant than American. One must expect exquisite courtesy one week and total forgetfulness the next, and learn to turn one’s back with the same unconscious indifference. Adams had nothing to complain of; he was treated better than in Boston.

By natural affinity, the social eccentrics sympathized with political eccentricity. The English mind took to rebellion—when foreign—and felt particular confidence in the Southern Confederacy. All the eccentrics rushed into the rebel ranks; few but well-balanced minds attached themselves to the Union. William E. Forster was a practical Yorkshireman; Cobden, considering the one-sided conditions of his life, well balanced; Bright stronger in expression, yet consistent and practical; Monckton Milnes’s fancies were only ideas a little in advance. The “cranks” were all rebels; the list portentous. The Church was rebel; the dissenters mostly with the Union. The universities were rebel; the public men who enjoyed confidence took infinite pains to be neutral for fear of seeming eccentric. The canny Scots and Yorkshiremen were cautious.

This eccentricity did not mean strength. Proof lay in the mismanagement of rebel interests. Why Jefferson Davis sent Mr. Mason to London when he sent Slidell to Paris, no one knew. Mason had common sense, perhaps, but in London society counted merely as one eccentric more. He might have figured as a new Franklin; instead he became the Minister’s bulwark of defence. Mr. Lamar, sent on a futile mission to St. Petersburg, had tact and humor, and would have done better in London; society would have delighted in him.

Surrounded by cranks of the worst English species, the rebels accepted as champion an eccentric of eccentrics, Mr. Roebuck—a sort of Brougham of Sheffield, with poor judgment and worse temper. With his doings the secretary had no concern except to report, on June 30, 1863, his motion to recognize the Confederacy. The Legation felt no anxiety, with Vicksburg in its pocket and Bright and Forster to say so; and Bright caught and shook Roebuck as a big mastiff shakes a wiry, bad-tempered terrier. Rebel allies, who had assured themselves that Bright would not cross swords with Roebuck again, learned—too late—that their sword-fish was getting the worst of it.

Whether British eccentricity were ever strength weighed heavily in education. The Southern people owed their ruin largely to the barbaric weakness of attributing want of courage to opponents; yet Bright’s courage was notorious. He struck, in succession, nearly every man in England who could be reached by a blow; if he could not reach the individual, he struck the class; if the class were too small, the whole people. He could not act on the defensive; he required attack.

On March 26, 1863, a Trades-Union meeting at St. James’s Hall, the result of patient effort to unite Bright and the Unions on an American platform, showed his method. With singular skill and oratorical power, he managed at the outset to insult every class commonly considered respectable, and, for fear of any escaping, insulted them again under consecutive heads. The rhetorical effect was tremendous:

“Privilege thinks it has a great interest in the American contest,” he began in his massive, deliberate tones; “and every morning with blatant voice, it comes into our streets and curses the American Republic. Privilege has beheld an afflicting spectacle for many years past. It has beheld thirty million of men happy and prosperous, without emperors—without king (cheers)—without the surroundings of a court (renewed cheers)—without nobles, except such as are made by eminence in intellect and virtue—without State bishops and State priests, those vendors of the love that works salvation (cheers)—without great armies and great navies—without a great debt and great taxes—and Privilege has shuddered at what might happen to old Europe if this great experiment should succeed.”

The audience cheered furiously. Ministers would be careful, once they saw Bright talk republican principles before Trades-Unions. Whether to class him as eccentric or conventional troubled the secretary. Every one called him “un-English,” from Palmerston to Forster; to an American he seemed more English than any of his critics. He was a liberal hater, and what he hated he reviled after the manner of Milton, but he feared no one. He almost alone hated Palmerston and was not afraid of him, or of press or pulpit, clubs or bench. He loathed the whole fabric of sham religion, sham loyalty, sham aristocracy, sham socialism. He had the British weakness of believing only in himself and his own conventions. In all this an American saw—if one may make the distinction—much racial eccentricity, but little that was personal. Bright was singularly well poised; but he used singularly strong language.
